bearings.paper_claim: Unit fixed-effects regressions are biased when treatment and time-varying covariates feed back on each other (citing Imai & Kim 2019 and Sobel 2012). The paper's remedy moves the fixed effects into a propensity model and requires a binary treatment that switches within units, a correctly specified parametric propensity model, and N and T growing together. Simulations use n of 200-3000 with T of at least 4; in the empirical panel, campaign windows run 8-40 weeks.
bearings.system_side: OLS of sector-year spending DVs (contributions_real_m; LobbyView lobbying for the L*-LV tests) on a growth term with sector FE plus controls (pres_year, midterm_year, exp_dem_house, exp_dem_senate), with year-FE variants (variant year_fe) and first-differences-with-year-effects (FDY) checks; inference is a wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector, DESCRIPTIVE when only 2 sectors. Reference values in the Codex review file sgs_review.R: L3-LV coefficient +0.352 (n=77) becomes -0.477 with year FE, and the FDY coefficient is -0.537 over 71 adjacent pairs (window and sample as set in that test's spec).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the diagnosis transfers, not the estimator. The study's regressor is continuous sector growth with few sector clusters and annual T, so IPTW-FE cannot run: no binary within-unit-switching treatment and no feasible propensity model. Read the paper as support for not interpreting the L-LV coefficients causally. A sign flip under added year FE is consistent with feedback or time-varying confounding, so neither sign is causal. Applies to any sector-year panel where lobbying or giving is the outcome of a growth regressor that may itself respond to past spending.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side holds: p.3 (lines 104-109) says feedback is usually ruled out by linear outcome FE estimators, citing Sobel 2012 and Imai & Kim 2019; binary D_it (line 183), within-unit switching (abstract), N,T grow at ratio rho (Theorem 1), simulations n in {200..3000}, n=200 T=4 (line 927-928), panel 8-40 weeks. Code side was overstated: no log giving/log lobbying DV (log1p is only a variant), no tossup, trend or lagged/AR lobbying term found in sgs_registry.R or sgs_estimate.R; the +0.352/-0.477/-0.537/71 values are in sgs_review.R (reference values), not a brain record, and -0.537 is FDY (first differences with year effects), not a 'first-difference lead'. Rewritten accordingly.

bearings.paper_claim: Placebo tests check the identifying assumptions by applying the estimator to outcomes measured before treatment: the previous election's vote share and turnout, and the pre-election poll share. IPTW-FE estimates are near zero, while the naive approach shows residual confounding for some Democratic-ad effects.
bearings.system_side: H1 is a Spearman correlation between the frozen seed_prob and new cosponsorships after the freeze. H2 is a Spearman correlation between pressure_mult and absolute tier movement. Both are cross-sectional, with no pre-freeze placebo. The contract requires at least 60 days and 150 movers, and returns UNDERPOWERED without consuming the look.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The placebo logic carries over directly. A pre-registered negative control would be Spearman(seed_prob, cosponsorship delta over a window that ends before the freeze). A non-zero value would show that seed_prob tracks a stable member trait (a time-constant confounder) rather than responsiveness. Adding it changes the contract, so it needs Paul's ruling before the single look is spent, and it needs a second pre-freeze snapshot pair. Neither H1 nor H2 measures a lobbying treatment, so even a PASS remains an association.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper: Section 6.4 (lines 1271-1325) uses previous-election outcomes for the same market/office and pre-five-week Dem poll share; both IPTW approaches near zero, naive shows some residual confounding for Democratic-ad effects. Code: outcome_contract.py PROTOCOL_TEXT (H1 Spearman seed_prob vs new cosponsorships, H2 pressure_mult vs |tier movement|), minimum 60 days and 150 members with a cosponsorship delta, returns UNDERPOWERED with look_consumed False (lines ~262-263), h1/h2 Spearman at ~277-278; no placebo/negative-control term in the file. The proposed negative control is the analyst's suggestion, needs Paul's ruling, UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Democratic interest-group TV ads raise the Democratic two-party share mainly by raising Democratic turnout, with a weaker negative effect on Republican turnout. Republican interest-group ads have no estimated effect on any outcome. The Democratic effect is concentrated after Trump's candidacy; the pre/post-Trump effect differences are significant at alpha 0.1 (no level is stated in the text for the pooled effects). No point estimates are given in the text.
bearings.system_side: potential = (wp x (1-|2s-1|) x t + (1-wp) x s x (1-t)) x (1 + wi x i). The weights on persuasion of undecided likely voters and on mobilization of supporters unlikely to vote are symmetric across parties, with module default wp 0.5 used only when the district entry names none (DEFAULT_WEIGHTS, untapped.py:53,71-73); no party term enters the formula.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The treatment is broadcast TV ads aggregated to the media market in Senate and gubernatorial races, 2010-2020. It is not door-to-door contact, and the outcome is not individual. The finding suggests that mobilization effects can dominate and can differ by party and era, so a fixed, party-symmetric wp is a judgment call that this paper neither validates nor sets. It does not transfer to US House districts (OR-05, CT-01) or to canvassing without field-experiment evidence.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper p.28 (lines 1118-1127): Dem IG ads positive on Dem performance, driven by Dem turnout, weaker negative on Rep turnout; Rep IG ads no effect. p.30: post-Trump concentration, era DIFFERENCES significant at alpha 0.1. Code: untapped.py docstring lines 9-10 give the formula exactly; wp default 0.5 is a fallback, per-district defaults may differ. Strength weak is right. Paper claim softened: alpha 0.1 applies to the era-difference tests (p.30), not stated for the pooled main effects.

bearings.paper_claim: Groups may target markets with more persuadable voters using a metric the researcher cannot see, so a naive comparison of treated and untreated units is confounded. The paper handles only time-constant unmeasured confounding, through unit fixed effects in the propensity score. Time-varying unmeasured confounding still breaks identification.
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0 x exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0) scales effective dollars on both money legs. AMPLITUDE and SCALE are Paul's judgment constants, uncalibrated, and the reciprocity they encode is explicitly NOT validated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: No direct transfer. The paper estimates effects of ads on voters, not the responsiveness of legislators to PAC dollars, and it must not be cited as support for c (D-104..D-108). Its only bearing is on calibration: any future attempt to estimate c from observed giving and alignment must handle strategic targeting of competitive seats, because givers pick those seats on information the analyst lacks.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper: line 228 (p.8) persuadable-voter targeting by a metric unknown to the researcher; Assumption 1 discussion (~line 356-361) says time-constant unmeasured confounding only, time-varying unmeasured confounding invalidates it. The p.32 citation concerns measured targeting on opponent negativity; minor. Code: moneyball_core.py:74-93 has c=1+AMPLITUDE*exp(-max(lean,0)/SCALE), AMPLITUDE 1.0, SCALE 5.0, both money legs, judgment constants, reciprocity NOT validated. Transfer correctly bars citing it as support for c (D-104..D-108).

related.why: Both papers question unit and two-way fixed-effects designs under feedback. Blackwell & Yamauchi cite the 2019 Imai & Kim paper on the same problem. Together they underwrite reading the sector-growth year-FE sign flip as non-causal.
Weimer uses Monte Carlo as a negative control. Blackwell & Yamauchi use placebo outcomes from before treatment. Both are falsification checks that the prospective contract lacks.

Both papers bear on campaign persuasion and its returns, and Broockman co-authored the Hewitt et al. (2024) experiments used here as a magnitude benchmark (1.2-2.3 pp). Together they inform Terrier's split between persuasion and mobilization.

Kalla's experiment identifies the effect of money on legislators' access. This paper identifies the effect of outside spending on voters. The flip model's money assumptions need evidence of the first kind, which this paper does not supply.

summary_issues: 'Effects are significant only at alpha 0.1' overstates the text: alpha 0.1 is stated only for the pre/post-Trump era DIFFERENCES (p.30, line ~1209). For the main Figure 3 effects the text says only that methods 'generally agree on the direction and significance', with no level given.

Bearing 1 system description (in rel, echoed by 'fixed-effects regressions of sector growth on spending') is reversed in direction: spending is the DV and growth the regressor; also log DVs, tossup/trend controls and a lagged/AR lobbying term were not found in the cited code, and the sign-flip values come from sgs_review.R reference values, not a brain record.
Gap item on Mentat's transfer graph (89% oppose IE split) was not verified here; treat as UNVERIFIED.
